header.name: Percolation Theory
header.description: The origin of the study of percolation theory in 1957 was to model the flow of a liquid through a random medium. Unlike stochastic processes where the motion is random while the medium is fixed, here the medium is random. Physicists adopted this model to describe many phenomenon, such as phase transition and formation of clusters, observed in statistical physics. Mathematicians studied this model because it not only has an honest application, but that the questions are easy to frame, but new techniques are required to understand them. In the 1990’s application of the mathematical theory developed over the three decades were used to study wireless transmission and network topology. This course will motivate students towards formulating models to understand real-life phenomenon. In addition to developing skills to study discrete phenomenon, it will also enable students to apply their knowledge from a diverse set of fields to answer questions.
prerequisites_mandatory: MTH 102: Probability and Statistics, or equivalent
MTH 371: Stochastic Processes and Applications, or equivalent.

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Determine how to model stochastically real-life phenomenon.

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Design methods to study discrete systems arising in physics.

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Explain random networks, something which is ubiquitous in modern times, like the wireless network, etc., using probabilistic parameters.

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: Deconstruct the notion of ergodicity which guarantees a stationarity not only in Markov processes but also in other dependent structures.

lecture_topics: Measure Theory Basics
Introduction to bond and site percolation.
Formal probability set-up
Critical phenomenon and its existence
FKG inequality, BK inequality (only for increasing events)
Russo’s formula
Exponential decay of the percolation probability below criticality
Uniqueness of the infinite open cluster
Critical probability for two dimensions is 1/2
Oriented percolation in two dimensions: Subadditive ergodic theory
Introduction and the model
Characterisation of pc
Recurrence properties of the right edge process
Exponential estimates for p < pc.
Proof of no percolation at criticality
Exponential decay of the time of ‘extinction’.
Continuum percolation (if time permits): The Boolean model
Coupling and scaling, FKG inequality
Occupancy in Boolean models
Vacancy in Boolean models, the covered volume fraction.

resources.title: R. Meester and R. Roy, Continuum Percolation
